item.title: Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
item.description:
Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.

The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.

Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.

Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.

Idriss Ghazi Kareem

Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.

The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.

Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The  Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.

“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”

The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.

Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.

“Floating coffins”

Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”

And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

item.title: Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
item.description:
Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.

The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.

Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.

The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.

When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.

The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.

Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”

Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

item.title: Lost Erasmus book returns to Rotterdam after 400 years
item.description:
Lost Erasmus book returns to Rotterdam after 400 years

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A book by Dutch Renaissance philosopher Desiderius Erasmus, which was thought to be lost, has been returned to Rotterdam after being identified by a collector in the US.

La civilité puérile (The Civility of Children) is a short collection of thoughts on good manners in children, printed in French in 1609.

The booklet contains rules such as: “It is downright ridiculous to make trumpet sounds with your nose: leave that to horn players and elephants.”

“If someone else sneezes, you must wish them good health (pay close attention to that)” is another piece of advice, along with “only sit down at the table after you have washed your hands, and cut your nails too.”

John Tholen, a curator at the Rotterdam Library, told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that getting the book back after four centuries was a very special event.

“We have found an unknown piece of the puzzle regarding the history and influence of Erasmus’s ideas,” Tholen said. “This copy is the only one left in the world from a print run of perhaps as many as 1,000.”

The UNESCO Erasmus Collection in Rotterdam holds more than 3,000 editions of the scholar’s works, plus another 3,000 books and articles about him published after 1900.

item.title: Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train
item.description:
Off the rails: a final goodbye to the Apekop train

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The iconic Apekop train, officially known as Mat ’64 (Materieel ’64), made its last journey on Wednesday before heading back into retirement.

Originally retired from service in 2016, the passenger train was brought back by operator Keolis last year, to the delight of train enthusiasts, to run between Amersfoort and Barneveld Zuid after refurbishment work on newer trains led to a rolling stock shortage.

But its 12.25pm departure from Barneveld Zuid on Wednesday is said to be its final trip. The train will now return to Stichting 2454CRW, a volunteer organisation that maintains old trains.

First appearing on Dutch tracks in 1961, the Mat ’64, the last NS train built largely in the Netherlands, came to symbolise Dutch commuter travel. The trains served passengers for more than five decades, with hundreds in service at their peak.

The nickname Apekop, which translates as “monkey head”, comes from the train’s distinctive rounded nose.

item.title: Health insurance could cost you €177 more next year
item.description:
Health insurance could cost you €177 more next year

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Healthcare premiums are set for their biggest rise in 15 years after insurer DSW announced its premium will go up by €14.75 a month in 2027.

The basic insurance package, which is compulsory for everyone, will cost €173.50 per month, or €2,082 a year.

DSW is traditionally the first Dutch health insurer to publish its rates for the following year, but all companies tend to follow a similar line because the content of the basic package is prescribed by law.

The rise of 9.3% is the largest in percentage terms since 2011, when premiums went up by 10%.

“In the eight years I have worked here I have never seen such a big increase,” Aad de Groot, chair of DSW’s board of directors, told broadcaster NOS.

It is also more than the €12.50 estimated by the health ministry in its budget calculations for next year. The maximum health benefit (zorgtoeslag) is going up by €11 a month for people earning the minimum wage, meaning low earners will have to pay more out of their own pockets for health cover.

The excess, or deductible, on health insurance is also going up for the first time in a decade. From January patients will have to pay the first €400 for treatment covered by the basic plan, up from the current level of €385.

De Groot said the government had not taken into account cuts to mental health care, hospital care and care at home in its calculations. “The effect is that the state is paying less but individuals are paying more through their premiums,” he said.

People whose earnings are just above the threshold for government support will be hit hardest, he added. Some 200,000 people have fallen behind on their insurance payments, according to the CAK, the government agency that handles healthcare bills, up from 172,000 in 2022.

“We see a growing group of people who are struggling to pay their premiums,” De Groot said. “It is a painful increase, but we have no option but to do this.”

Insurers must publish their rates by November 12, after which Dutch residents have until the end of the year to decide whether to switch to a different insurer for 2027.

item.title: European Commission investigates Booking over scams
item.description:
European Commission investigates Booking over scams

October 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The European Commission has launched an investigation into whether Amsterdam-based travel site Booking.com has breached data protection laws by not cracking down on fake adverts.

The Brussels-based commission will also consider whether the company told site users which adverts had been ranked higher in search results because their owners had paid more, as is required under transparency rules.

In a third branch of the investigation, Booking.com is accused of exposing users to phishing scams by hackers who gained access to the company’s reservation and guest data.

Booking.com could be hit with fines amounting to 6% of its turnover if the commission decides it has breached the rules and refuses to change its policies.
The number of scams reported on the website increased by 500% between 2022 and 2024, with fraud totalling €4.2 billion in 2024 alone.

Henna Virkkunen, European commissioner for tech sovereignty, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed.”

In a statement, Booking.com said it was “cooperating fully” with the investigation, adding: “security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities.”

“We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners,” the company said.

item.title: Feyenoord second best to Betis as Isco is on the spot for CL win
item.description:
Feyenoord second best to Betis as Isco is on the spot for CL win

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord endured a frustrating evening in Spain as a penalty by Real Betis’s outstanding player, Isco, secured a 1-0 win for the La Liga side.

The Rotterdammers were second best for most of the game, but held out until the 59th minute, when Abde Ezzalzouli’s cross hit the arm of Jeremiah St. Juste in front of goal.

Isco, who was at the heart of Betis’s attacks all evening, grabbed the ball and gave Tjark Ernst no chance from the penalty spot.

Ernst had made good saves from former AZ Alkmaar striker Troy Parrott and Marc Batra to keep Feyenoord in the game in the first half, but Feyenoord had the best chance of the opening period when Gjivai Zechiël shot over the bar from close range.

The visitors had a claim for a penalty of their own turned down in the 68th minute when Givairo Read claimed he had been pushed by Ezzalzouli, but referee Simone Sozza waved the appeals away.

The result leaves Giovanni van Bronckhorst’s side in 26th place in the Champions League table, with Internazionale up next in De Kuip on November 3.

item.title: Some important websites remain down after emergency shutdowns
item.description:
Some important websites remain down after emergency shutdowns

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Websites in the Netherlands are coming back online following emergency shutdowns. This follows the discovery of vulnerabilities in the programming language on which many government, hospital and news sites are built, including Dutch News.

The organisation behind PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, said on Tuesday it would patch two flaws in its code.

The announcement prompted hackers to search for the holes and begin trying to attack sites, which US cyber security firm Cloudflare said on Wednesday it was noticing and defending against.

Sites were then swiftly taken down, including the government’s digital ID system DigiD and its online services portal MijnOverheid, the website of parliament, the umbrella organisation for the water boards, and a tool used by local councils for storing documents and scheduling meetings.

Some important sites, like anonymous crime reporting site Meld Misdaad Anoniem and domestic safety reporting network Veilig Thuis, were still offline on Thursday morning.

Disruptions
Dutch media companies were hit – RTL’s news website and app went down, and broadcaster NPO shut down the system used to upload content to its streaming services.

Several hospitals also took their websites down, as well as charities such as KWF cancer fund and the Dutch Heart Foundation.

Schiphol airport’s app stopped showing live flight information, and benefits agency UWV took a tool people use to report sick or recovered offline.

The problem was not limited to the Netherlands – the Flemish, German, French and Finnish governments all took websites offline.

What happened
Two critical flaws in PHP’s programming language were discovered in August using AI models from OpenAI and Google.

Google-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz, one of the firms that reported the flaws to PHP, said that the vulnerabilities in PHP had existed for over a decade, and said they ranked “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

PHP built fixes for the vulnerabilities into an update and said all companies using its code should install the update immediately. Prime minister Rob Jetten reiterated this call on social media.

Justice minister David van Weel said the fact that so many websites had been taken offline as a precaution “has an impact on our digital society”.

“Fortunately, there are currently no indications that the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited,” Van Weel stated through his spokesperson.

The National Cyber Security Centre said it had not seen any active hacks, and the PHP Foundation told news agency ANP it also had no indication of breaches.

item.title: Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age
item.description:
Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of Dutch workers who stay in work beyond the statutory retirement age has increased by more 50% in eight years, according to latest figures from the statistics agency CBS.

In the second quarter of this year 152,000 people in work were over the age of 67, representing 1.7% of the working population.

In the first quarter of 2018 1.2% of workers were beyond the retirement age, which was then 66, equivalent to 96,000 people.

Men are more likely than women to keep going to work after drawing their pension, the figures show. In June 2.3% of men over 67 were working, compared to 1.1% of women.

The figures also revealed large differences between sectors, with 4.3% of people working in real estate after their 67th birthday compared to 0.6% of civil servants.

A study by the demographic institute NIDI in 2023 found that most people who kept working in retirement did so because they enjoyed their job or to feel useful. Just 10% said the need to earn money was a significant factor.

The Netherlands has the latest retirement age in the European Union, along with Denmark, Sweden, Italy and Greece. The state pension age is due to increase to 67 years and three months in 2028.

item.title: Minister refuses inquiry into abuse at youth home in Spain
item.description:
Minister refuses inquiry into abuse at youth home in Spain

October 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Long-term care minister Mirjan Sterk has refused to launch an independent investigation into a Dutch youth care scheme in which children are sent abroad, despite revelations about exploitation and harsh treatment.

An investigation by news programme Nieuwsuur found that the “family home” in the Valencia region, which has been running for over 20 years, subjected children living there to cruel physical and psychological punishments.

Sending troubled teenagers abroad is a long-standing practice in Dutch youth care, meant to remove them from difficult environments in the Netherlands. Huize Soria alone received tens of millions of euros in taxpayers’ money over 20 years, according to the investigation.

Reporters found that the Dutch owners of Huize Soria, the Valencia institution, were forcing children their to work long hours. When they misbehaved, they were deprived of food, sleep and access to a toilet.

Some were made to stand stress positions for long periods, others said. Contact with relatives in the Netherlands was restricted, sometimes for months at a time.

Experts described the conditions as “torture”. Huize Soria was ordered to close down in September after evidence of abuse was first uncovered.

Sterk, from the centrist Christian Democrat CDA, has urged youth care organisations to stop placing Dutch children abroad where possible said there was no need for her to order an investigation.

In a letter to parliament, she said it was up to local councils, child protection agencies and care providers who placed the children to make sure the home met the rules.

She also said she did not know which organisations had sent children to Huize Soria, apart from one child protection agency, because there is no central record.

MPs from across the political spectrum said that was exactly why an investigation was needed. Far-right JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie said refusing one was “running away from your responsibilities”.
